primary_cause: No clear Microsoft-specific negative. Broad-market liquidation in mega-cap tech after Fed emergency move failed to restore confidence. Teams usage surged later in week (positive)
secondary_factors: Fear of weaker enterprise IT budgets. PC demand disruption. General de-risking of high-liquidity growth names. S&P 500 fell ~12%
store_description: This looks much more like an index-and-liquidity event than a Microsoft event. On March 16 the market was repricing an abrupt global recession and Microsoft as one of the largest and most liquid tech names got used as a source of cash despite later evidence that remote-work demand was boosting Teams users.

primary_cause: Severe semiconductor selloff on recession and supply-chain fears. No major Micron-specific negative release
secondary_factors: Concerns global consumer and electronics slowdown would hit memory pricing and demand. Pre-earnings anxiety ahead of Micron late-March report
store_description: Micron's nearly 20% drop was steeper than the market because memory names were viewed as highly cyclical and very exposed to a sudden collapse in global manufacturing and end demand. On March 16 investors were pricing a hard stop in consumer and industrial activity.

primary_cause: No material NextEra-specific negative. Liquidity-driven selling even in defensive utilities. Cross-asset scramble for cash
secondary_factors: Recession fears around commercial and industrial electricity demand. Financing sensitivity in yield-oriented utility and renewables names
store_description: NextEra was hit less than cyclical tech or retail but it still sold off because March 16 was not a normal defensive rotation day. It was a cross-asset scramble for cash. Even rate-sensitive utility leaders were repriced lower.

primary_cause: Not earnings-driven. Oracle reported fiscal Q3 Mar 12 with non-GAAP EPS $0.97 up 11%. Overwhelmed by Mar 16 market panic
secondary_factors: Concern enterprise software bookings and on-premise IT spending would weaken in recession. S&P 500 fell ~12%
store_description: Oracle is one of the clearest cases where company news was not the culprit. The stock fell almost 11% despite an earnings release showing non-GAAP EPS up 11% and no obvious company-specific blow-up which strongly points to indiscriminate selling and sudden repricing of enterprise-spending risk.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Nike said Mar 15 would close all stores in U.S. and several other markets Mar 16-27 to slow the virus
secondary_factors: Global recession fears. Supply-chain disruption. Sharp weakness in discretionary consumer spending. Broader collapse in retail foot traffic
store_description: This one had a real stock-specific catalyst. Investors were suddenly forced to model lost in-store sales across Nike's own retail footprint just as the broader market realized shutdowns could spread nationwide so the stock's 11.6% fall was more than just passive market beta.

primary_cause: No clear negative ServiceNow-specific announcement. De-rating of high-multiple software amid forced selling
secondary_factors: Concern new enterprise deals and implementation cycles would slow in shutdown economy. Market discounting sudden freeze in corporate decision-making
store_description: ServiceNow's drop was milder than semis or retail which fits the pattern of a quality software name being hit mainly by multiple compression rather than a company-specific shock.

primary_cause: No major Merck-specific negative. Broad healthcare selloff during market-wide liquidation
secondary_factors: Fear fewer doctor visits and procedure delays would weigh on pharma demand channels even for high-quality defensive names
store_description: Merck's move looks mainly macro rather than idiosyncratic. On March 16 investors were selling even traditionally defensive healthcare stocks because the priority was raising cash and reducing exposure not hiding in stable earnings franchises.

primary_cause: Semiconductor and high-beta tech liquidation. No major Nvidia-specific negative. Earlier shifted GTC to online-only Mar 2
secondary_factors: Fear of data-center capex caution gaming demand disruption and supply-chain interruptions. Market applying severe recession haircut to cyclical tech
store_description: Nvidia traded like a classic high-beta semiconductor growth stock in a crash session falling 18.5% even though the most notable recent corporate news had been conference disruption not a profit warning.

primary_cause: No Netflix-specific negative. Indiscriminate equity liquidation. In hindsight stay-at-home beneficiary but market not rewarding nuanced winners on Mar 16
secondary_factors: Temporary concern about production disruption. General de-risking of growth equities
store_description: In hindsight Netflix was a stay-at-home beneficiary but on March 16 the market was not rewarding nuanced winners. It was selling almost everything. The stock's 11.1% drop reflects broad liquidation pressure and uncertainty about production schedules.

primary_cause: No meaningful new Altria-specific negative. Broad-market selloff. Relatively modest 4.6% decline fits defensive staple
secondary_factors: Continued overhang from vaping and Juul mess. General consumer-staples de-risking. Systemic liquidation day
store_description: Altria's relatively modest 4.6% decline versus the market fits a defensive staple with existing company baggage but no fresh catalyst in the 72-hour window. The stock likely fell mainly because March 16 was a systemic liquidation day.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Reuters reported McDonald's and Starbucks closing dine-in areas at many U.S. stores shifting to takeaway and delivery. Local and state restrictions on restaurants intensifying
secondary_factors: Franchisee stress. Commuting collapse. Recession fears. Direct hit to restaurant traffic from dine-in shutdowns
store_description: McDonald's had a genuine operating catalyst. Once dine-in service began shutting down across major U.S. markets investors had to reprice same-store sales franchise cash flow and the duration of mobility restrictions which explains why MCD underperformed the broader market.

primary_cause: Anticipation that small-business advertising budgets would crater in shutdown economy. No fresh Facebook-specific negative. Reuters confirmation COVID hurting advertising came later Mar 24
secondary_factors: Broad tech liquidation. Concern over global ad demand. Travel local commerce events and many small businesses shutting down threatening ad budgets
store_description: Even before Facebook explicitly said ad sales were weakening the economic logic was obvious by March 16: travel local commerce events and many small businesses were shutting down which threatened ad budgets. Macro-to-company transmission effect not a single discrete Facebook headline.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Kaiser Permanente announced Mar 16 would postpone all elective or non-urgent surgeries and procedures. Directly relevant to Medtronic device volumes
secondary_factors: Hospital capacity being redirected to COVID care. Wider healthcare-system disruption. Rapid postponement of elective procedures
store_description: Medtronic had a real fundamental COVID hit because many of its products are tied to procedures hospitals suddenly began delaying. Once big systems started pausing elective work the market could infer a near-term revenue shock for device makers.

primary_cause: No major fresh Mondelez-specific negative. Earlier Reuters in January flagged Chinese factory closures and Q1 pressure. Broad consumer-staples selloff in market-wide cash scramble
secondary_factors: Concern about international operations supply-chain friction and weaker away-from-home and snacking channels
store_description: Mondelez was not being repriced because of a new 72-hour headline so much as because investors were suddenly discounting global disruption everywhere at once. The stock's double-digit decline suggests staples were not immune when the market shifted from selective fear to systemic liquidation.

primary_cause: Expected collapse in travel-related and discretionary payment volumes. Travel bans restaurant shutdowns and social-distancing orders already implying severe hit to cross-border and discretionary card spending
secondary_factors: Recession risk. Lower consumer spending. Cross-border weakness. No direct Mastercard warning in prior 3 days but business-model exposure obvious
store_description: Mastercard's business model is highly exposed to transaction activity especially profitable cross-border travel spend. With gatherings canceled borders tightening and restaurants and leisure shutting down investors were effectively front-running the transaction slowdown that card networks later confirmed.

primary_cause: Semiconductor equipment crash on fears of capex retrenchment and supply-chain disruption. No Lam-specific negative release
secondary_factors: China and global fab uncertainty. High-beta tech deleveraging
store_description: Lam fell almost in line with other semiconductor names because investors assumed customers would slow equipment spending and the global chip supply chain would seize up. The move looks sector-driven rather than tied to any Lam announcement.

primary_cause: No Lowe's-specific negative. Extreme brick-and-mortar retail panic as shutdowns spread. Market not yet appreciating home improvement would later prove resilient
secondary_factors: Fear of store traffic collapse. Consumer retrenchment. 24.8% drop one of hardest-hit names. Investors treating physical retail as if widespread closures and demand destruction imminent
store_description: Lowe's was one of the hardest-hit names because on March 16 the market was treating physical retail as if widespread closures and demand destruction were imminent. The later pandemic-era home-improvement boom was not visible yet.

primary_cause: No Lockheed-specific negative. Industrial and defense selloff inside broad liquidity event. Concern about supply-chain disruption
secondary_factors: Indiscriminate selling of large-cap industrials. Business normally more defensive than commercial aerospace which is why double-digit drop points to systemic stress
store_description: Lockheed's business is normally more defensive than commercial aerospace which is exactly why this kind of double-digit drop points to systemic stress more than company news. Investors were selling what they could not just what had deteriorating fundamentals.

primary_cause: Actually POSITIVE news — Lilly and AbCellera announced Mar 12 would co-develop antibody therapies for COVID-19. Broad healthcare and market selloff not stock-specific bad news
secondary_factors: General concern about recession and drug-market disruption offset partly by Lilly COVID therapeutic collaboration
store_description: Lilly is another case where the company-specific headline in the window cut the wrong way for a bearish explanation: the major news was constructive not negative. That makes the stock's 7.2% drop look mainly like collateral damage from the March 16 panic.

primary_cause: Recession repricing for industrial gases and manufacturing-linked demand. No major Linde-specific negative. Global industrial shutdown fears
secondary_factors: Broad selling in cyclical industrials. Products deeply tied to industrial activity healthcare and manufacturing end markets
store_description: Linde's products are deeply tied to industrial activity healthcare and manufacturing end markets so a sudden global stop in production was enough to hit the stock even without a discrete company event. The move looks primarily like a macro demand-shock repricing.
